rows.text:
Modern family forms (nuclear, extended, single-parent) — know the terms.
Discuss change vs continuity: roles shift, emotional bonds remain.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ## The grammar of memory Family stories are told in the past, and the past has three doors. The **simple past** for the single event ("grandfather told his stories after dinner"). **Used to** and **would** for the repeated rituals of a childhood ("we *would* fall asleep before the ending; we *used to* fight over the one pillow").…  ·  ## The comparison that examiners set every year Joint family or nuclear family — the question arrives in different clothes every session, and the answer that stands out is the one that argues functions, not forms. Houses change; the jobs a family does — care, teaching, feeding, belonging — do not.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## How the exam asks it Three shapes recur. The **comparison essay** ("Which family suits modern Nepal?") wants a thesis in the first paragraph, two or three criteria from the table above, one concession, one restatement. The **personal recount** ("A family member who influenced me") wants one scene per paragraph, past-tense discipline, and the influence stated once, plainly, at the end — not announced in the first…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. How does the text portray the bond between generations? (2 marks) — affection mixed with duty and misunderstanding; cite one exchange.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Q. Should elderly parents live with their children? (2 marks) — balanced answer: companionship and care vs independence; end with your view.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The words that carry the theme English sorts families by shape and the shapes have exact names. A **nuclear family** is parents and children; a **joint family** is several generations sharing one roof and, more tellingly, one kitchen; an **extended family** is the wider web of grandparents, uncles and aunts who may live nearby rather than together; a **single-parent family** and a **blended family**…  ·  ## Reading the theme like a writer — the devices of family writing Family writing lives or dies on **showing versus telling**. "My mother is very caring" is a report; "my mother still texts the family group before every exam, a habit she started with my sister's first test twelve years ago" is a portrait.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Family questions in this unit revolve around generational change — contrast the text's family values with modern urban life in one paragraph.  ·  Trick 2: Character questions: show the character through DIALOGUE, then interpret the relationship dynamic it reveals.

rows.text: Q. Should elderly parents live with their children? (2 marks) — balanced answer: companionship and care vs independence; end with your view.
